title: How to analyze data with AI
description: Collect what you need, get a defensible answer out of what you have, settle the definitions people argue about, and show the working.
introduction: Almost nobody's data problem is the analysis. It's that the export quietly dropped cancelled orders, two dashboards define an active user differently, and the join duplicated eleven percent of the rows. The maths was never the hard part.

So the useful thing isn't a tool that runs a regression. It's one that looks at the file properly before it answers, tells you what it found, and shows the working behind every number so you can reproduce it without asking how it was made.

sections.title: Get an answer out of what you have

blocks.text: The most valuable thing here usually isn't the analysis. It's catching the reason the analysis would have been wrong. So the file gets inspected before anything is calculated, and you hear what turned up:

items: What one row actually represents, which is not always what the column headers suggest.
Missing values, and whether they're missing at random or in a pattern that means something.
Duplicates, and whether they're genuine repeats or a join that went wrong.
Numbers stored as text, mixed date formats, and the other quiet type problems.
Outliers, which are either errors or the most interesting thing in the dataset.

blocks.text: You get told that before you see a chart. Finding out about a broken join afterwards means you've already half-believed the answer.

Then the working shows: which filters were applied, which rows were excluded and why, and the formula behind any figure that matters. And what the data shows stays separate from what it implies. A drop in signups the same week as a price change is a correlation with a good story attached, and it gets labelled as one.

items.context: Analyze this dataset for the question I need answered.

blocks.text: Sometimes the dataset you need isn't anywhere. It's spread across a few hundred pages that each hold one row of it. Strawberry works in the browser, so it can go and get those fields, validate them as it goes, and hand back a table with a source against each row.

items.context: Collect these fields across these sources into a clean table.

blocks.text: Most arguments about numbers are really arguments about definitions. What counts as active. Whether the month is calendar or rolling. Which timezone the day ends in. Two tools can both be right and still disagree.

Because your companion works across the logged-in tools you already have open, it can compare how each one defines the same metric rather than taking one dashboard's word for it. That's usually where the discrepancy turns out to live.

items.title: Reconcile conflicting numbers
items.text: Work out why two sources disagree, and which definition should win.

skill.context: Reconcile how these metrics are defined across sources.

items.title: Check the framework itself
items.text: Decide whether you are measuring the right things before optimising the numbers.

skill.context: Review whether this metric framework is measuring the right things.

blocks.text: An analysis nobody acts on may as well not have run. Once the findings are accepted, they can become a presentation that leads with the answer and keeps the evidence traceable underneath it.

items.context: Turn this accepted analysis into a presentation.

blocks.text: Most analysis meets its real test in a meeting, where someone asks why this number disagrees with the one in their dashboard. Turning up with the definitions already reconciled is the difference between a review and an ambush.

items.title: Walk in with the numbers
items.text: The current figures, what moved since last time, and the questions people are likely to ask.

skill.context: Prepare me for this metrics review.

items.title: Capture what was decided
items.text: The decisions, the follow-up questions, and the analysis someone still owes.

skill.context: Turn this review into decisions and follow-ups.

items.title: Write the recurring update
items.text: A concise, accurate update for the people who need the numbers but were not in the room.

skill.context: Turn the current numbers into an update.

blocks.text: Recurring reports have a habit of drifting. The definitions move slightly, someone applies a different filter, and two quarters stop being comparable without anyone deciding that.

Once a report is right, the definitions, filters, quality checks, and output can be saved so next period runs the same way. If several people build versions of the same thing, that accepted method can be shared instead.

items.context: Turn this report into something the team runs the same way every period.

blocks.text: When it genuinely repeats on a schedule, it can become a Routine that pulls the data, runs the same checks, and brings you the result to review.
